steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React and useState into your file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the necessary imports to start building your Mini Redux app.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported React and useState, which are essential for building React components with state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import statement. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty fragment for now.
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns an empty React fragment (<> </> or <React.Fragment> </React.Fragment>).
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a functional App component that returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is defined and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named exactly 'App' and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Create a function called App that returns an empty fragment.

steps.title: Initialize Redux-like state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create an initial state object with a property called 'count' set to 0.
steps.hint: Define a constant variable (e.g., 'initialState') at the top of your component function body. The object should look like: { count: 0 }.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a constant variable representing the initial state of your Redux-like store.
successCriteria: An 'initialState' (or similar) object is defined with a 'count' property set to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the initial state object that will serve as the foundation for your Mini Redux store.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a state object, but make sure it has a 'count' property set to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: The initial state object with 'count: 0' is missing. Create a constant variable with this structure inside your component.

steps.title: Create the reducer function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'reducer' that takes two parameters: 'state' and 'action'. Inside the function, use a switch statement on 'action.type' to handle 'INCREMENT' and 'DECREMENT' cases, returning a new state object with an updated 'count' property.
steps.hint: The reducer should return a new state object with the count increased by 1 for 'INCREMENT' and decreased by 1 for 'DECREMENT'. Don't forget a default case that returns the current state unchanged.
steps.expectedOutcome: A reducer function is defined that can handle 'INCREMENT' and 'DECREMENT' actions to update the count in state.
successCriteria: The reducer function is defined with 'state' and 'action' parameters, uses a switch statement on 'action.type', handles 'INCREMENT' and 'DECREMENT' cases, and returns a new state object with updated count.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the reducer function that follows the Redux pattern. This function will be the core of your state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your reducer handles both 'INCREMENT' and 'DECREMENT' actions and returns a new state object rather than mutating the existing one.
steps.feedbackWrong: The reducer function isn't quite right. Remember it should take 'state' and 'action' parameters, use a switch statement on 'action.type', and return a new state object for each action type.

steps.title: Set up React state with initial state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'state' and initialize it with the initial state object you defined earlier.
steps.hint: Call useState with your initial state object as the argument, and destructure the returned array into two variables: the state variable and a setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: useState with an object
const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'Alex', age: 25 });
steps.expectedOutcome: The useState hook is called with the initial state object, creating a state variable and setter function.
successCriteria: A useState call is added that initializes a state variable with the initial state object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected your Redux-like state to React's component state using useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useState with the initial state object and destructuring the result into two variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using useState correctly. You need to call it with your initial state object and destructure the returned array.

steps.title: Create dispatch function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named 'dispatch' that takes an action object as a parameter. This function should call the reducer with the current state and the action, then update the React state with the result.
steps.hint: The dispatch function should be defined inside the component. Use the reducer you already created and the state setter from useState.
steps.expectedOutcome: A dispatch function is defined that will handle action dispatch and state updates.
successCriteria: The dispatch function is defined, calls the reducer with current state and action, and updates React state with the result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the dispatch function that will handle actions and update state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your dispatch function calls the reducer and updates the React state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The dispatch function isn't quite right. It should take an action, call the reducer with current state and action, then update the React state.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, replace the current return value with a div element that has className 'app' and contains an h1 with the text 'Mini Redux Demo'.
steps.hint: The return statement should now return JSX with a div wrapper containing a heading.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div with class 'app' containing an h1 with the title 'Mini Redux Demo'.
successCriteria: The JSX includes a div with className 'app'
The div contains an h1 element with text 'Mini Redux Demo'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the main container structure for your Mini Redux demo.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have a div with className 'app' containing an h1 with the exact text 'Mini Redux Demo'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return statement should be replaced with a div containing an h1. Check the structure and text content.

steps.title: Display current count state
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the current count value from the state object.
steps.hint:
Use JSX to render a

tag with the count value inside curly braces, like {state.count}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a value from state

Current value: {state.value}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current count value (initially 0) in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added to the return statement that displays the count from state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the current count from state in the UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're displaying the count value from the state object inside a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element displaying the count from state is missing or incorrect.

steps.title: Add increment button and wire dispatch
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a dispatch function that takes an action object and updates the state using the reducer.
steps.hint: Define a function called dispatch that takes an action parameter, calls the reducer with current state and action, and uses setState to update the state with the result.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a dispatch function that can process actions and update the component state.
successCriteria: A dispatch function is defined that calls the reducer with current state and action, then updates state with setState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your dispatch function is ready to handle actions and update state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your dispatch function calls the reducer and uses setState to update the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The dispatch function is missing or incomplete. It should take an action, call the reducer, and update state with setState.

steps.title: Add decrement button and wire dispatch
steps.instruction: Add a second button with the text 'Decrement' that calls dispatch with an action object { type: 'DECREMENT' } when clicked.
steps.hint: Place the new button after the increment button in the JSX. Use the same dispatch function you created earlier.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: adding another button with a click handler
<button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'DECREMENT' })}>
  Decrement
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will have two buttons: 'Increment' and 'Decrement'. Clicking 'Decrement' will reduce the count by 1.
successCriteria: A button with text 'Decrement' is present and calls dispatch with { type: 'DECREMENT' } when clicked.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've completed the Mini Redux implementation with both increment and decrement actions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it calls dispatch with the correct action type 'DECREMENT'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The decrement button is missing or not properly wired to dispatch.
